cultural_notes: Woccon is a Siouan language
The Woccon people lived in North Carolina
Knowledge of Woccon derives primarily from John Lawson's book 'A New Voyage to Carolina', first published in London in 1709
Woccon people are mentioned in documents dealing with the Tuscarora War of 1711-1713
The original Woccon vocabulary was documented in the first edition of Lawson's work held at the British Library
Woccon is a Siouan language related to Catawba
The Woccon lived in two villages on the lower Neuse River in what is today southern Greene and northern Lenoir Counties
Lawson estimated the Woccon population at 120 fighting men, making them the second most populous tribe of the North Carolina coastal plain after the Tuscarora
The Woccon were located between the Tuscarora and European settlements of Bath and New Bern
There is no historical record of the Woccon after the Tuscarora War ended in 1713
Surviving remnants of small coastal plain tribes were likely absorbed by the more populous Tuscarora
Lawson's book contains a vocabulary of 143 items in the Woccon language
Lawson noted that Woccon, Tuscarora, and Pamlico languages differed in every word except one: Tsaure (cockles)
Tuscarora is an Iroquoian language and Pamlico is an Algonquian language
The first attempt to relate Woccon with Catawba was made by Adelung and Vater in 1816
Lawson also used the spellings Waccon and Wacon for the tribe name
Woccon and Catawba languages were suggested to be genetically related by Adelung and Vater based on similarities in vocabulary comparisons
Gallatin concluded in 1836 that Woccon and Catawba were genetically related, finding sixteen words with affinities out of fifty-one compared words
